source: Hart, Nilsson, Raphael (1968) A formal basis for the heuristic determination of minimum cost paths (via Wikipedia A*)
finding: A* was built at SRI for the Shakey robot. It ranks open nodes by f = g + h, cost so far plus estimated cost to go. Nilsson's earlier Graph Traverser ignored path cost; Raphael added g; Hart added admissibility and consistency.
numbers: Published 1968. The PDF copy fetched was a scan with no text, so the original was not read; facts come from the Wikipedia article.
limits: Secondary source for the founding paper. The 1968 optimal-efficiency claim was shaky.
agent_relevance: S6 ranking should score a child by cost so far plus estimated remaining cost, not by estimated remaining cost alone.

source: Wikipedia A* search algorithm: admissibility and optimality
finding: A* is optimal if h never overestimates true cost to goal (admissible). Proof idea: the open list always holds a node on an optimal path whose f cannot exceed the optimum, so a worse goal is never closed first.
numbers: Complete and optimal on finite graphs with non-negative edge weights. Dijkstra is A* with h = 0.
limits: Needs non-negative costs and a true lower bound. Inadmissible h loses the guarantee.
agent_relevance: An S6 scorer that overestimates remaining work can prune the right branch. Use optimistic (low) estimates when optimality matters.
quote: A* is admissible when its heuristic is admissible, meaning it never overestimates the true cost to the goal.

source: Wikipedia A*: consistency and Dechter-Pearl optimal efficiency
finding: Consistent h obeys h(x) <= d(x,y) + h(y). Then A* never reopens a node. Dechter and Pearl (1985) proved A* with a consistent heuristic expands the fewest nodes among admissible A*-like algorithms on non-pathological problems. A 1972 'correction' claiming consistency was unneeded was shown false in 1985.
numbers: Result holds for consistent h only. For admissible but inconsistent h other algorithms can expand arbitrarily fewer nodes.
limits: Optimal efficiency counts the set of nodes expanded, not loop iterations.
agent_relevance: Scores that are monotone along a path make revisits unnecessary. Cache and do not re-score closed states.

source: Wikipedia A*: complexity and weighted A*
finding: Worst case A* expands every node with f <= C* (optimal cost). Time and space O(b^d); space is the main limit, which led to IDA*, SMA*. Weighted A* uses e*h with e > 1 and returns a path costing at most e times the optimum.
numbers: Bound O(C*/epsilon) with epsilon the smallest gap between f values. Weighted A* bound: cost <= e * optimum.
limits: Inconsistent heuristics can cause many re-expansions, but mostly in contrived cases.
agent_relevance: Greedy weighting trades quality for speed with a known worst-case loss. A budgeted agent can pick the weight on purpose.

source: Wikipedia Heuristic (computer science): Pearl 1984 definition
finding: A heuristic function ranks alternatives at each branching step. For a graph, h(v,goal) is admissible if h <= true distance d*. A non-admissible h can fail to reach the goal, by hitting a dead end or oscillating between two nodes.
numbers: Cites Pearl (1984) Heuristics: Intelligent Search Strategies for Computer Problem Solving as the source only; no Pearl numbers on the page.
limits: Wikipedia citation only. Pearl's book itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: The oscillation failure is a real risk for an LLM scorer: two children that each rank the other higher. Needs a visited set.

source: Newell and Simon (1976) Computer science as empirical inquiry: symbols and search (via Wikipedia Heuristic)
finding: Heuristic search hypothesis: a physical symbol system solves problems by generating and changing symbol structures until one matches the solution. Possibilities judged unlikely to lead to a solution are never generated.
numbers: Turing Award lecture, CACM 19(3):113-126. No experiment numbers.
limits: Hypothesis, not a measured result. The original lecture was not opened; claim comes via the Wikipedia article.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema idea: do not expand everything, filter children before they cost tokens.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: deliberate problem solving with large language models
finding: Tree of Thoughts lets a GPT-4 agent propose several next thoughts, score them with the model, and keep the best b by BFS or DFS. Game of 24 jumped from 4% with chain-of-thought to 74% with breadth 5.
numbers: Game of 24 (100 hard puzzles, GPT-4, May 2023): IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC k=100 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%, CoT best of 100 49%, IO best of 100 33%.
limits: Only 100 puzzles, one model family, tasks with short depth (3 steps). Evaluator is the same model that generates.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for ranking children at S6: a value call per child beat 100 blind samples.
quote: In Game of 24, while GPT-4 with chain-of-thought prompting only solved 4% of tasks, our method achieved a success rate of 74%.

source: Yao et al. (2023) ToT: where chain-of-thought fails
finding: About 60% of CoT samples on Game of 24 had already failed after the first step (first three words). Left-to-right decoding commits early with no way to rank alternatives.
numbers: Figure 3b error analysis, Game of 24, GPT-4.
limits: Single task.
agent_relevance: Rank first-step choices explicitly; the first step is where most of the loss happens.

source: Yao et al. (2023) ToT: generator vs evaluator ablation
finding: With GPT-3.5, ToT on Game of 24 reached only 19% (vs 74% GPT-4). Mixed setups: GPT-4 generates + GPT-3.5 evaluates gave 64%; GPT-3.5 generates + GPT-4 evaluates gave 31%. The bottleneck was generating good thoughts, not scoring them.
numbers: Appendix B.2. 3-shot proposal prompt used for GPT-3.5.
limits: Small test set; evaluator quality tested at only two levels.
agent_relevance: A cheap model can rank children if a strong one proposes them. Spend strong-model tokens on proposal.

source: Yao et al. (2023) ToT: cost
finding: ToT cost about as much as 100 CoT trials but won. Per case: ToT 5.5k completion + 1.4k prompt tokens at 74%; CoT best-of-100 6.7k + 2.2k at $0.74 and 49%; IO best-of-100 $0.13 at 33%.
numbers: Game of 24 cost table. Creative writing: ToT about 5x tokens of CoT; humans preferred ToT in 41 of 100 pairs, CoT in 21, 38 ties; GPT-4 coherence 7.56 vs CoT 6.93 vs IO 6.19.
limits: API prices of mid 2023.
agent_relevance: Equal token budget favours scored search over blind resampling on tasks with clear step validity.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with language model is planning with world model (RAP)
finding: RAP makes the LLM both world model and agent and uses Monte Carlo tree search with a reward mix (action likelihood, state confidence, self-evaluation). On Blocksworld with LLaMA-33B, RAP(20) solved 100% of 2-step, 88% of 4-step, 42% of 6-step; CoT solved 17%, 2%, 0%.
limits: Blocksworld only, small step counts; reward weights set by exploratory tuning; action-likelihood reward matters for planning but not for math.
agent_relevance: A tracked world state lets the agent see which moves are legal and back out. Matches a code-held state.

source: Zhou et al. (2023/2024) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS)
finding: LATS runs MCTS with an LLM value function plus self-consistency as part of the heuristic. HumanEval Pass@1: GPT-3.5 CoT 46.9, ReAct 56.9, Reflexion 68.1, ToT 54.4, RAP 63.1, LATS 83.8; GPT-4 Reflexion 80.1, LATS 92.7 (GPT-4 baseline 91.0).
numbers: Game of 24, GPT-3.5: CoT 0.08, Reflexion 0.12, ToT 0.20, RAP 0.40, LATS 0.44. HotPotQA EM ablation: ToT 0.39, RAP 0.54, LATS no LM heuristic 0.37, LATS DFS 0.42, no reflection 0.58, full 0.63.
limits: The gain over a strong GPT-4 baseline on HumanEval is small (91.0 to 92.7; the 91.0 row label was read from table text and may belong to another method). Self-reflections were generic on WebShop.
agent_relevance: Removing the LM heuristic dropped HotPotQA from 0.63 to 0.37, so the ranking signal carries the gain.

source: Lehnert et al. (2024) Beyond A*: better planning with transformers via search dynamics bootstrapping (Searchformer)
finding: A transformer trained on A* execution traces (create/close tokens with g and h values) then fine-tuned on shorter correct traces solved 93.7% of Sokoban test tasks with 26.8% fewer search steps than the A* used to make its data.
numbers: Sokoban, 200 test tasks: fine-tuning cut incorrect and non-optimal solution rates by 40% and 30%; A* traces were 34.3% longer after 3 fine-tune rounds. Heuristics: Manhattan distance in mazes; sum of box-dock Manhattan distances in Sokoban.
limits: Trained from scratch on synthetic mazes and Sokoban. Traces reach near 100000 tokens and can grow exponentially with plan length.
agent_relevance: A model can imitate and then beat the symbolic search it learned from, but training costs are large. Not a prompt-only result.

source: Lehnert et al. (2024) Searchformer: trace training vs solution-only
finding: Models trained on A* search traces beat models trained on answers only, mainly with little data and harder tasks. The smallest search-augmented model beat a much larger solution-only model; a 175M search-augmented model slightly beat a 747M solution-only model on Sokoban.
numbers: Over 90% of test mazes: thousands of trace tokens with no wrong token. Gap widest at 50,000 training sequences and in larger mazes.
limits: Synthetic domains; any-optimal-64 scoring gives higher numbers than exact match.
agent_relevance: Writing out the search (frontier, closed set, scores) helps more than writing only the answer, if the trace is checkable.

source: Meng et al. (2024) LLM-A*: LLM enhanced incremental heuristic search on path planning
finding: LLM-A* lets an LLM propose waypoints that guide A* cost estimates. On 50x30 grids, GPT-3.5 cut operations to 57.39% and storage to 74.96% of plain A*, with +2.44% path length; LLaMA3 cut operations by 44.59% and storage by 64.02% (+2.47% path length). Valid path ratio 100%.
numbers: Example map: A* 859 operations, 802 storage, length 53.46; LLM-A* 140, 235, 53.46. Dynamic weighted A* (w=2) was worse than LLM-A* on both. LLM-only planning was worse in validity and length. About 90% of LLM-A* paths were optimal.
limits: Not guaranteed optimal. Grid maps only. Waypoint heuristic is inadmissible in principle.
agent_relevance: Pattern to copy: model suggests where to look; sound code still does the search and checks validity.

source: Xiao et al. (2023) LLM A*: human in the loop LLM enabled A* search for robotics
finding: A short 2023 paper that combined A* with an LLM that gives the global direction, plus a human in the loop. Metrics: search complexity (open + closed set size), path length, and a smoothness count of back-and-forth moves (MDT).
numbers: Paper compares with A* and a PPO baseline on small grid maps; exact table values were not extracted.
limits: Small demonstrator. Numbers not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Early example; the 2407.02511 paper is the better-measured version.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Q*: improving multi-step reasoning for LLMs with deliberative planning
finding: Q* uses A* with f(s) = g(s) + h(s), where h is a learned plug-and-play Q-value model scoring the next reasoning step, so the LLM policy is not fine-tuned. Reported gains on GSM8K, MATH and MBPP over MetaMath-style baselines.
numbers: GSM8K base Llama-2-7b MetaMath 65.2%; Q* row near 80.8% (read from table text, could be misaligned). MBPP with CodeQwen1.5-7b: Q* about 55.4% (table text).
limits: Needs a trained Q-value model. Table parse of numbers is rough; treat as approximate.
agent_relevance: Shows the A* form f = g + h applied to reasoning steps. The h is learned, so not admissible.

source: Lu et al. (2021) NeuroLogic A*esque decoding: constrained text generation with lookahead heuristics
finding: Decoding with a lookahead estimate of future constraint satisfaction, in the spirit of A*, replaced beam search. It set new state of the art on table-to-text, constrained machine translation and keyword-constrained generation.
numbers: Five generation tasks; gains largest in few-shot or zero-shot settings and with many constraints. Exact scores not extracted.
limits: Constraint-based generation, not reasoning.
agent_relevance: Lookahead scoring beats left-to-right scoring when future constraints matter.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) On the planning abilities of LLMs: a critical investigation
finding: GPT-4 generated valid goal-reaching plans for only about 34% of 600 Blocksworld instances, 206/600 to 214/600 depending on prompt style. LLM plans used as seeds for the LPG local-search planner kept about half their steps in the final plan.
numbers: Blocksworld: GPT-4 34.3% to 35.6%. Human study: 39 of 50 participants (78%) made a valid plan.
limits: Static 2023 models. Domain obfuscation drops accuracy heavily.
agent_relevance: LLM plans are weak as final answers but useful as seed heuristics for a sound repair search.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs can't plan, but can help planning in LLM-Modulo frameworks
finding: Position paper: LLMs are approximate idea generators, not planners. Pair them with external verifiers in a generate-test loop (LLM-Modulo) that guarantees soundness.
numbers: Position paper, ICML 2024; no new benchmark.
limits: Argument rather than experiment.
agent_relevance: Fits guardrail G2/G3: the model proposes, code verifies.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) Planning in strawberry fields: o1 on PlanBench and scheduling
finding: o1-preview solved 97.8% of 600 Blocksworld instances (3-5 blocks) but only 23.63% of 110 instances needing 20+ steps. Best plain LLM, LLaMA 3.1 405B, got 62.6% on Blocksworld and under 5% on Mystery Blocksworld.
numbers: o1-preview on Sokoban (55 instances): 12.7%; o1-mini 10.9%. TravelPlanner sole-planning: prior best 4.4% (GPT-4-turbo), o1-preview barely above. Graph coloring o1-mini 96% vs 16% GPT-4 in prior work.
limits: Cost per query high; correctness not guaranteed; long-horizon drop.
agent_relevance: Search done inside the model still decays with plan length; external search keeps its guarantee.

source: Hao et al. (2025) LLMs can solve real-world planning rigorously with formal verification tools
finding: Letting the LLM write code for an SMT solver gave 93.3% (validation) and 93.9% (test) final pass rate on TravelPlanner, against about 10% for the best direct LLM (o1-preview). Paraphrased prompts: 86.7% with GPT-4.
numbers: Greedy search without a formal spec: 0 passes. Other baselines 0.6%, 4.4%, 10.0%. Interactive plan repair succeeded on 63.7% of 39 UnsatChristmas queries.
limits: Needs hand-written instruction steps and code; tuned on travel domain.
agent_relevance: Sound solver beats model-led search when constraints are formal. Model should translate, code should search.

source: Katz et al. (2024) Thought of Search: planning with language models through the lens of efficiency
finding: Having the LLM write only the successor function and goal test, then running ordinary BFS or DFS, solved Game of 24 (1361 of 1362 solvable puzzles found), 5x5 crosswords, Blocksworld and PrOntoQA at 100% with a few LLM calls. ToT and RAP are neither sound nor complete.
numbers: Code needed 1.2 interactions for 24-game successors, 2.4 for crossword successors, 2.8 for Blocksworld. ToT claimed 75% on 100 medium 24-game problems. ToT at bound 100 uses up to 200 calls per crossword game.
limits: Task needs a checkable state model; heuristics left to future work.
agent_relevance: Strongest critique: do not pay LLM calls per node when a short program expands nodes for free.

source: Koh et al. (2024) Tree search for language model agents
finding: A best-first tree search over live web states with a GPT-4o value function raised VisualWebArena success to 26.4% (39.7% relative gain) and WebArena to 19.2% (28.0% relative gain).
numbers: Search params d=5, b=5, c=20 node expansions. Success rose with budget c in {0,5,10,15,20} and with depth and breadth. A re-ranking baseline plateaued near 30% on a 200-task subset, below search at c=5 as the paper states. VWA: 910 tasks; WA: 812 tasks.
limits: Needs ability to undo or reset the environment; compute budget limited; value model is the same LM.
agent_relevance: Search value rises with budget but one needs reversible states. Ranking children by value plus budget caps worked.

source: Korf (1997) Finding optimal solutions to Rubik's Cube using pattern databases
finding: IDA* with pattern-database lower bounds found first optimal solutions to random Rubik's Cube instances. Median optimal length is about 18 moves. State space 4.3252e19. Manhattan-style heuristic has expected value 5.5; pattern databases raise it to 8.764 (corner table), 8.878 (max of three).
numbers: Corner table 42 MB; three tables total 82 MB. Search speed about 700,000 nodes per second on a Sun Ultra-Sparc 1. Old heuristic reaches depth 14 in about 3 days; depth 18 would take over 250 years. Conjecture: time x space = size of state space.
limits: Specific to Rubik's Cube; the time-space law was a hypothesis. Pattern databases are from Culberson and Schaeffer (1996), tested on the 15-puzzle.
agent_relevance: Heuristic strength is measured by its mean value over the space. A better lower bound is worth more than more search.

source: Korf (1997): heuristic expected value and IDA* cost
finding: If every state had heuristic value e, IDA* to depth d would equal brute-force iterative deepening to depth d - e. The prediction is too low because IDA* visits states biased toward small heuristic values.
numbers: Branching factor 18 before pruning repeated moves, 15 after the first move (further reduced by commuting-move pruning).
limits: Formula is an estimate, not exact.
agent_relevance: Each point of average heuristic value saves a depth level; this gives a rule for how much a ranker is worth.

source: Hoffmann (2003) The Metric-FF planning system: ignoring delete lists (FF heuristic)
finding: FF builds its heuristic by relaxing the planning task: ignore the delete (negative) effects of actions, then estimate the length of a relaxed plan. Search is forward state-space search guided by that estimate. FF is a close relative of HSP (Bonet and Geffner).
numbers: Describes the 2001 FF system and its numeric extension; this paper reports many IPC domain results, not extracted.
limits: The relaxed-plan estimate is not admissible in general.
agent_relevance: Domain-independent way to derive a ranker: ask what the remaining work would cost if side effects did not matter. Shows how to build h for S6 without a learned scorer.
